g1: A free-body diagram is a picture of the forces on one object. Today you will draw one yourself.
g3: Name the object first. Draw each force from that object and label its source.
g4: Choose the asteroid. Later you will decide which objects push or pull on it.
g5: Find where velocity is zero. Read the slope there to tell whether the cart still accelerates.
g6: The arrows help you find net force. You need the net force before you can find acceleration.
g7: Look at the crate. Name what touches it and what pulls on it from far away.
g8: Draw the phone as a dot. Ask what the desk does and what Earth does.
g9: Match each arrow to a source. The floor can push up and also exert friction sideways.
g10: Start all arrows at the dot. A longer arrow means a larger force when you use one scale.
g11: Say the object, list its interactions, then draw. Use this order each time.
g12: Check the source, direction and length of each arrow. Remove arrows for forces on other objects.
g13: Draw rope tension up and weight down. The lamp stays at rest, so make the arrows equal in length.
g14: The table pushes the book up. Earth pulls it down. Both arrows belong on the book.
g15: The falling ball speeds up. Its downward weight must exceed the upward air resistance in this example.
g16: After the hand lets go, remove its push. Keep the forces that still act on the sliding box.
g17: Start the timer. The scribe draws one scene at the board. Each group member checks an arrow and saves their own answer.
g18: Components are parts of one force. Use the parts or the whole in a sum. Counting both would count the force twice.
g19: Ask what could cause a rightward push. The cart’s motion alone cannot supply one.
g20: Draw each object separately. Check what still touches it and which way friction acts.
g21: Trace the rope to the lamp. Label its upward pull and Earth’s downward pull.
g22: Gravity points toward its source. A contact force belongs on the asteroid only while the spacecraft touches it.
g23: Cross out a velocity arrow and an extra net-force arrow. Neither names a separate interaction.
g24: For the moving box, label weight, support, tension and sliding friction. Point each arrow the way that force acts.
g25: A moving asteroid needs no forward force just to keep moving. Draw the gravitational pulls in the model.
g26: Point to each arrow. Say who exerts that force, on what object and in which direction.
g27: Draw the final box diagram by yourself. Check its arrows before you submit.

q1: Draw the diagram for the resting book on comic page 57. Add an arrow for each force. Label its source and use the sizes on the page.
q2: A box slides right on a rough, level floor after a hand lets go. Name the forces that still act. Why does the hand no longer get an arrow?
q3: At the top of the toss on page 58, someone erases every arrow because the ball’s vertical velocity is zero. Check their diagram. Ignore air resistance.
q4: On page 59 a car turns at steady speed on a level road. A student draws friction inward and a second inward force called centripetal force. Which arrow should stay? Explain.
q5: On your own, draw the four forces on the moving box from page 60. Use the given sizes. Label each force with its source and point it in the correct direction.
a1: Earth pulls down and the table pushes up, each with 19.6 N on the book.
a2: Earth pulls down, the floor pushes up, and sliding friction acts left. The hand has lost contact.
a3: Keep weight downward. The hand has let go and air resistance is ignored. Zero vertical velocity at one instant does not remove gravity.
a4: Keep static friction inward. It provides the inward net force. An extra arrow would count it twice.
a5: Draw rope tension right, floor friction left, floor support up and Earth’s pull down. Match the lengths to the values on the page.
